lessonTitle: On-Call Work: Prioritising Tasks, Calling for Senior Help and Handing Over

blocks.text: It is 22:15 and you are the only foundation doctor covering three wards. Your list has eleven jobs, the switchboard has bleeped you twice, and a relative has been waiting at the nurses' station for forty minutes. Nobody can do all of it at once, so what separates a safe on-call doctor from an overwhelmed one is the method used to choose what to do next.

blocks.markdown: **Prioritisation** is the deliberate ordering of tasks so that the patients at greatest risk of harm are dealt with first. Two ideas drive the ordering. **Urgency** is how soon the task must be done before harm occurs (minutes, an hour, by the morning). **Risk** is how bad the harm would be, and how likely, if the task is delayed or missed. A task that is both urgent and high risk goes first; a task that is neither can wait or be handed over. Your list also changes as new bleeps arrive, so re-prioritise whenever new information comes in.

blocks.title: Time-critical task
blocks.text: A task where a delay beyond a defined window carries a real risk of harm, such as a first dose of antibiotics in suspected sepsis, insulin for a patient with diabetes, or a missed dose of a medicine whose timing matters (for example in Parkinson's disease or after a transplant). Local policy defines the windows; check the current guidance in your trust.

blocks.markdown: A practical order of work is: (1) any patient who may be in immediate danger (airway, breathing, circulation, a new reduction in consciousness, or a high early warning score), (2) time-critical treatments and results that will change management within the hour, (3) tasks that can be completed within the shift, and (4) routine or administrative tasks, such as discharge summaries, which can be handed over. Ask three questions of every job: what is the worst plausible outcome if I delay this, how soon could that happen, and could someone else safely do it? Delegating well, for example asking a nurse to start an agreed protocol or asking a pharmacist about an unavailable medicine, is itself a prioritisation skill.

rows: Airway, breathing or circulation threatened; marked physiological abnormality
Stridor, new unresponsiveness, severe hypotension, low blood glucose with drowsiness (new reduction in consciousness)
Go now; call for help early; use the emergency team where needed
Harm likely if delayed beyond a short window
Overdue time-critical medicine, a result needing action within the hour
Do or delegate within the hour; confirm completion
Needed before the shift ends but not threatening
Rewriting a drug chart, reviewing a stable patient with new pain, a requested blood test
Plan a time; record on the task list
Discharge summary for tomorrow, non-urgent referral letter
Do when free or hand over with a clear owner
blocks.caption: A working scheme for sorting concurrent tasks; local wording and time windows vary.

blocks.title: Sorting five concurrent jobs
blocks.prompt: At 21:00 you have five jobs: (a) a nurse reports that a 61-year-old man, 1 day after laparotomy, has new systolic BP 84 mmHg and pulse 126 per minute; (b) a request to write regular laxatives for another patient; (c) a discharge summary for tomorrow; (d) a patient with suspected cholangitis who needs a new cannula because the intravenous antibiotics are due in 40 minutes; (e) a relative on the phone asking for an update. Put them in order and justify the order.

steps.text: Identify the job with possible immediate danger: job (a) describes hypotension and tachycardia after major surgery, which could mean bleeding, sepsis or another cause of shock, so it is first. Go to the patient and call your senior early.

Identify the time-critical job: job (d) has a clock on it, since the antibiotics are due in 40 minutes and need venous access. Ask a nurse or healthcare colleague with cannulation skills to site it while you attend job (a), and confirm it is done.

Rank the rest by consequence of delay: job (b) is low risk and can be done in the same shift, and job (c) is for tomorrow and can be handed over. Job (e) matters to the family but does not alter immediate safety; ask a nurse to tell the relative you will call back at a stated time.
State the final order and the way you will record it on your list, including the time you will revisit each outstanding job.

blocks.answer: Order: (a) first, with (d) delegated at the same time, then (b), then (e) at a stated time, and (c) last or handed over. Justification: threat to life first, then a task with a deadline, then by consequence of delay.

blocks.markdown: **Calling for senior help.** Asking for help is a professional responsibility, not a failure. Escalate when a patient meets a local trigger (for example a high early warning score), when the patient is not responding to the initial treatment you have given, when you are unsure of the diagnosis or plan, when a task is outside your competence, or when something simply worries you. **Call early rather than late**: a senior can always say that you were right to be cautious. Call the right person by the local route, which might be the registrar, the consultant on call, the critical care outreach team or the emergency team. If the person does not answer, escalate to the next person in the chain of command and do not wait for a reply while the patient deteriorates.

items: Situation: who you are, where you are calling from, the patient, and the problem right now.
Background: the reason for admission, relevant history, current treatment and the treatment escalation plan if there is one.
Assessment: the latest observations and early warning score, your findings and your impression of how sick the patient is.
Recommendation: what you want, for example 'please come and see the patient within 15 minutes', and by when.
Check understanding, record the time of the call, the name of the person and the plan, then act on it.

blocks.title: SBAR gives you a script when you are anxious
blocks.text: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation works because it forces you to finish with a clear request. Have the observations, the drug chart and the notes to hand before you phone, and state the recommendation plainly rather than hoping the listener will infer it.

blocks.markdown: **Handover and documentation.** Handover is the transfer of responsibility for patients and tasks to the next team and is a high-risk moment for omission. Safe handover is structured (for example SBAR or a similar tool), takes place in a quiet protected space where possible, combines verbal and written information, and identifies the sickest patients and the active escalation plan first. Each task should have a named owner, a time and a contingency ('if the result is abnormal, then call the registrar'). The receiver should repeat back the key points to close the loop. Under the General Medical Council's Good medical practice, records should be clear, accurate, legible and made at the same time as the events or as soon as possible afterwards; each entry should carry the date, time, your name, grade and signature or identifier, and local policy sets the exact rules.

blocks.title: Writing a safe task handover
blocks.prompt: A patient in bay 3 had a low sodium on the evening blood test and the plan is to repeat the sodium at 02:00 and act on the result. You finish at 21:00. Write a handover entry the night team could act on, and explain what makes it safe.

steps.text: Start with identification: patient name, hospital number, bay and bed, so the right patient is found even when staff change.
State the task and the reason in one sentence: 'Repeat sodium at 02:00, because the evening result was low and the plan is to monitor the trend.'
Add the owner and the time: 'Night F1 to take blood at 02:00 and review the result.' Time and owner stop the task being assumed done by someone else.

Add the contingency: 'If the sodium is lower than on the evening test or the patient becomes drowsy or confused, call the medical registrar for review.' Add the escalation plan status and who is contactable.
Close the loop by asking the receiving doctor to read the task back and by leaving your name and the time on the entry.

blocks.answer: A safe entry contains the patient identifiers, the task and reason, a named owner and time, an if-then contingency and a read-back; vague notes such as 'check bloods overnight' are not safe.

blocks.title: Do not defer an unwell patient to the morning
blocks.text: If a patient is worrying you at the end of your shift, hand them over verbally and face to face, name them first, and make sure a senior or the incoming team has accepted responsibility before you leave. A written note alone, left on a desk, is not a handover.

points: Prioritise by urgency and risk: immediate danger first, then time-critical treatment, then tasks for the shift, then routine work.
Call early for senior help using SBAR and finish with an explicit recommendation; if there is no reply, go up the chain.
Safe handover and documentation use structure, a named owner, a time, a contingency and a read-back.
Records should be contemporaneous, clear, accurate, dated, timed and signed; check the policy of your trust.

questions.stem: At 02:00 you have four requests at once. Which should you attend to first?

options.text: A pending blood result that has not been reviewed yet and is not flagged as critical
A request for a night sedative from a patient who cannot sleep
A request to rewrite a patient's drug chart that is illegible
A patient who is anxious and breathing noisily, with a high-pitched sound on inspiration

questions.correctOptionText: A patient who is anxious and breathing noisily, with a high-pitched sound on inspiration

distractorRationale.a: Can be reviewed after urgent problems are dealt with.
distractorRationale.b: Low immediate risk and can wait for a review.
distractorRationale.c: Important, but not urgent and low immediate risk.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: possible airway compromise is the highest immediate risk.

questions.explanation: Noisy, high-pitched breathing on inspiration suggests partial upper airway obstruction, and airway problems kill quickly, so this sits in the immediate band. The other jobs are legitimate but low in risk and urgency, and can be delegated or done afterwards.

questions.stem: Two calls arrive together. A nurse says a ward patient with diabetes has a capillary blood glucose of 2.1 mmol/L and is drowsy; another nurse says a post-operative patient with a stable early warning score is asking for stronger analgesia for pain of 4 out of 10. What is the best response?

options.text: Ask the first nurse to recheck the glucose in an hour
Ask both nurses to wait until you have cleared your task list
Ask the first nurse to start the hypoglycaemia protocol now and go to that patient first, arranging the analgesia review for afterwards
Finish the analgesia review first because pain is distressing

questions.correctOptionText: Ask the first nurse to start the hypoglycaemia protocol now and go to that patient first, arranging the analgesia review for afterwards

distractorRationale.a: Delays treatment of a possible neuroglycopenic emergency.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a drowsy, hypoglycaemic patient is urgent and the protocol can begin while you travel.
distractorRationale.d: Pain matters but the hypoglycaemic patient is at greater immediate risk.

questions.explanation: A glucose of 2.1 mmol/L with drowsiness is severe hypoglycaemia and can progress to seizures or coma, so it is both urgent and high risk. Asking a trained nurse to start the local protocol, then attending, uses delegation to treat sooner, and the less urgent analgesia review follows; check the protocol in your trust.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the clearest reason to call your senior immediately?

options.text: A discharge summary that has been requested for tomorrow
A patient continues to deteriorate despite the initial treatment you have started
A request to chart a regular dose that is already on the drug chart
A routine blood test result that is within normal limits

questions.correctOptionText: A patient continues to deteriorate despite the initial treatment you have started

distractorRationale.b: Correct: failure to respond to first-line treatment is a core trigger to escalate.

questions.explanation: Failure to improve after initial treatment means the working diagnosis or plan may be wrong or the patient needs a higher level of care, and a senior should be involved without delay. Routine results and administrative requests do not require urgent senior input.

questions.stem: You are the foundation doctor covering medicine overnight. A 55-year-old man with known alcohol-related liver disease has vomited fresh blood twice. His pulse is 122 per minute, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, and he is pale and sweaty. Write the SBAR you would give when you phone the medical registrar.
markingGuide: Situation: introduces self, ward, patient name and the problem (haematemesis with tachycardia and hypotension)
Background: known alcohol-related liver disease, reason for admission, current medicines, escalation status

Assessment: observations and early warning score, appearance (pale, sweaty), impression of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding with shock and what has been started (ABCDE, access, blood tests including crossmatch per local protocol)
Recommendation: asks for urgent bedside review within a stated time and a plan, and asks whether to activate the major haemorrhage pathway or critical care involvement
Closes the loop: repeats the agreed plan, records time, name and plan in the notes
questions.explanation: The vignette is consistent with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding with hypovolaemia, which needs urgent senior review and resuscitation. Credit goes to a concise, ordered call that ends with a clear request and a documented plan, with any management decisions checked against local protocols.

questions.stem: You have called the on-call registrar twice about a deteriorating patient and had no reply. What is the best next step?

options.text: Manage the patient alone until the morning ward round
Leave a message on the ward whiteboard for the day team
Wait another 30 minutes and try the same registrar again
Escalate to the next senior in the chain, such as the consultant on call, and use the emergency or outreach team if the patient continues to deteriorate

questions.correctOptionText: Escalate to the next senior in the chain, such as the consultant on call, and use the emergency or outreach team if the patient continues to deteriorate

distractorRationale.a: Not appropriate for a deteriorating patient beyond your competence.
distractorRationale.b: A written note is not an escalation.
distractorRationale.c: Delays care for a patient who is deteriorating.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: do not wait; use the chain of command and the emergency route.

questions.explanation: Safe practice means the patient is never left without appropriate senior help because one person is unavailable. You escalate through the local chain of command and use the emergency or critical care outreach team, as local policy dictates, and document the attempts and times.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a safe written handover of a task?

options.text: It lists every test the patient has ever had
It is memorised and passed on in the corridor without writing it down
It names the patient and location, the task and why, the person responsible, the time, and what to do if the result is abnormal
It says 'check bloods overnight' next to the bed number

questions.correctOptionText: It names the patient and location, the task and why, the person responsible, the time, and what to do if the result is abnormal

distractorRationale.a: Too much unprioritised information buries the task.
distractorRationale.b: Prone to omission and not auditable.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: includes identifiers, owner, time and a contingency.
distractorRationale.d: Vague: no owner, time or action threshold.

questions.explanation: A handover entry should let a doctor who has never met the patient find the right person, understand the task and act correctly. A named owner, a time and an if-then plan prevent tasks from being assumed done, while a vague entry is a classic route to a missed result.

questions.stem: Entries in the medical record should be made at the time of the event or as soon as possible afterwards, and be dated, timed and signed so that the author and their role can be identified.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Good medical practice from the General Medical Council expects clear, accurate, legible records made contemporaneously, and an entry that cannot be attributed or timed is of limited use. Local policy sets the exact formats, so check the standard in your trust.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is nil by mouth after a bowel obstruction is suspected. His time-critical medicine is now 90 minutes overdue and he has become rigid and distressed. Which task should be prioritised among four jobs: this patient, a discharge summary for tomorrow, a relative's request for a call back, and normal bloods awaiting review?

options.text: The patient with the overdue time-critical medicine, seeking a safe alternative route with the pharmacist or senior
The normal bloods awaiting review, because results must always be seen in order
The relative's call back, because they are waiting
The discharge summary, because it is due soonest

questions.correctOptionText: The patient with the overdue time-critical medicine, seeking a safe alternative route with the pharmacist or senior

distractorRationale.a: Correct: omission of time-critical medicines can cause serious harm.
distractorRationale.b: Normal results carry little risk if reviewed later.
distractorRationale.c: Courtesy matters but the risk of harm is lower; delegate or schedule.
distractorRationale.d: Its deadline is tomorrow and the risk is low.

questions.explanation: Parkinson's medicines are the classic example of time-critical drugs, and missed doses can lead to severe rigidity, swallowing problems and complications. Prioritisation by urgency and risk puts this first, with advice from pharmacy or a senior on a safe alternative route, while the low-risk jobs wait.

questions.stem: At 23:30 you are the only doctor covering three wards. Your list is: a patient who is more breathless than at the evening review, a request for a urinary catheter to be reviewed, a night-time prescription for a regular antibiotic that is due at midnight, a relative's call and a discharge summary. Explain how you would prioritise, delegate and hand over, and when you would escalate.
markingGuide: Priority 1: the breathless patient (reassess ABCDE, observations, early warning score) and call senior early if worsening
Priority 2: the time-critical antibiotic prescription so that the midnight dose is given on time
Delegate suitable tasks (for example to a nurse or healthcare colleague) while checking competence and recording it
Priority 3: catheter review within the shift; relative's call back at a stated time; discharge summary handed over to the day team
Escalate to the senior if workload exceeds safe capacity or if a patient deteriorates
Re-prioritise as new bleeps arrive and keep the list updated
Handover at the end: verbal and written, sickest first, named owners, times and contingencies; document actions
questions.explanation: The top priority is the possibly deteriorating patient, followed by the time-critical medicine, then work that can be done later in the shift, delegated or handed over. A strong answer shows a method, explicit use of delegation and escalation, and a handover that leaves no task without an owner and a time.

questions.stem: At 20:55 you are due to hand over at 21:00. A patient you reviewed at 20:30 has a rising pulse and a senior has not yet seen him. Which action is the safest?

options.text: Wait until the senior reviews him in the morning handover
Mention him last in a corridor handover because he has not yet been seen
Hand over verbally and face to face to the night team, naming this patient first with the escalation plan, and stay until a senior has accepted responsibility
Leave a written note on the desk and go home on time

questions.correctOptionText: Hand over verbally and face to face to the night team, naming this patient first with the escalation plan, and stay until a senior has accepted responsibility

distractorRationale.a: Unsafe delay for a patient who may be deteriorating.
distractorRationale.b: The sickest patient must be first in the handover.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the sickest patient is handed over first and responsibility is explicitly transferred.
distractorRationale.d: A note alone is not a handover and leaves the patient unattended.

questions.explanation: Handover is a high-risk transition, and a patient who may be deteriorating must be named first, with the escalation plan and a clearly identified owner. Staying until a senior has taken responsibility is consistent with professional duty, while a note or a vague mention risks the problem being lost.
